questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL)?
options: ML is a subset of DL, which is a subset of AI
DL is a subset of ML, which is a subset of AI
AI is a subset of ML, which is a subset of DL
AI, ML and DL are independent, non-overlapping fields
questions.why: AI is the broad field of building systems that perform tasks requiring intelligence; ML is the part of AI that learns from data; DL is the part of ML that uses multi-layer neural networks. Option A reverses the inner nesting: plenty of ML (e.g., decision trees) is not deep learning.

questions.q: A retail analyst has purchase histories for 2 million customers but no labels, and wants to discover natural customer segments. Which learning paradigm fits?
options: Supervised classification
Reinforcement learning
Supervised regression
Unsupervised clustering
questions.why: With no target labels, the goal is to find structure in the data itself, which is what clustering (e.g., k-means) does. Supervised classification would need predefined segment labels for training, which the analyst does not have.

questions.q: A logistics team wants a model that predicts the delivery time of each parcel in minutes. What type of ML task is this?
options: Regression
Binary classification
Clustering
Multi-class classification
questions.why: Predicting a continuous numeric quantity is regression. It would become classification only if the target were discretized into categories such as "on time" vs "late".

questions.q: Which description best fits reinforcement learning?
options: Learning a mapping from inputs to labels using an annotated dataset
Grouping unlabeled examples by similarity
An agent learning a policy by taking actions in an environment to maximize cumulative reward
Reconstructing masked parts of the input from the rest of the input
questions.why: RL is defined by an agent, actions, an environment, and a reward signal that may be delayed. Option A is supervised learning; the RL agent never receives a "correct action" label, only rewards.

questions.q: Pretraining a language model to predict the next word in raw web text is an example of which paradigm?
options: Supervised learning with human-annotated labels
Self-supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Semi-supervised clustering
questions.why: In self-supervised learning the training targets are derived automatically from the data itself (here, the next word), so no human labeling is required. It looks like supervised learning mechanically, but the labels are not human-annotated, which is what makes it scalable to web-sized corpora.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a validation set?
options: To provide additional training examples once the training set is exhausted
To report the final, unbiased performance of the chosen model
To store mislabeled examples for later cleaning
To tune hyperparameters and select between candidate models
questions.why: The validation set guides decisions such as learning rate, model size, or when to stop training. Because those decisions are fitted to it, it is no longer unbiased; that role belongs to the held-out test set (option B).

questions.q: A team evaluates on the test set after every hyperparameter change and keeps the best configuration. What is the problem?
options: The test set has become part of model selection, so its score is optimistically biased
The test set is too small to be used more than once mathematically
Evaluating on the test set updates the model weights
There is no problem; this is the recommended workflow
questions.why: Repeatedly choosing configurations by test score effectively tunes on the test set, so the reported score no longer estimates performance on unseen data. Evaluation does not change weights (option C); the leakage happens through the human selection loop.

questions.q: During training, training loss keeps falling while validation loss starts rising after epoch 6. What is happening?
options: Underfitting
The learning rate is too low
Overfitting
Data drift in the training set
questions.why: A widening gap where training loss improves but validation loss worsens means the model is memorizing training-specific patterns that do not generalize. Underfitting would show both losses remaining high.

questions.q: A linear model has high error on both the training and validation sets. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Add stronger L2 regularization
Use a more expressive model or add informative features
Reduce the size of the training set
Apply more dropout
questions.why: High training and validation error indicates underfitting (high bias), which is fixed by increasing model capacity or giving the model better features. Stronger regularization and dropout reduce capacity further and would make underfitting worse.

questions.q: In neural network training, what is an epoch?
options: One complete pass of the training algorithm over the entire training dataset
One update of the weights from a single mini-batch
The time it takes to run validation once
The number of layers in the network
questions.why: An epoch means every training example has been seen once. A single weight update from one mini-batch is called an iteration or step (option B); an epoch usually contains many steps.

questions.q: A training set has 10,000 examples and the batch size is 250. How many optimizer steps make up one epoch?
questions.why: Steps per epoch = dataset size / batch size = 10,000 / 250 = 40. The value 400 comes from dividing by 25 instead of 250, a common slip.

questions.q: Training loss jumps around wildly and occasionally becomes NaN within the first few hundred steps. What is the most likely cause?
options: Batch size too large
Too few epochs
Learning rate too high
Too much training data
questions.why: A learning rate that is too large makes updates overshoot the minimum, so the loss oscillates or diverges to NaN. Too few epochs would leave loss high but stable, not erratic.

questions.q: In gradient descent, in which direction are the parameters updated?
options: In the direction of the gradient of the loss
In the direction opposite to the gradient of the loss
Perpendicular to the gradient of the loss
In a random direction scaled by the loss value
questions.why: The gradient points toward steepest increase of the loss, so gradient descent steps along the negative gradient: θ ← θ − η∇L. Following the positive gradient (option A) would be gradient ascent and increase the loss.

questions.q: Which loss function is the standard default for a regression model predicting house prices?
options: Mean squared error
Binary cross-entropy
Hinge loss
Categorical cross-entropy
questions.why: MSE averages the squared differences between predicted and true continuous values, making it the typical regression loss. Cross-entropy losses compare probability distributions over classes and are meant for classification.

questions.q: A model classifies support tickets into 12 mutually exclusive categories. Which loss function is most appropriate?
options: Mean absolute error
Mean squared error on the class index
Contrastive loss
Categorical cross-entropy
questions.why: Cross-entropy over a softmax output penalizes low probability on the correct class and is the standard loss for mutually exclusive multi-class problems. Regressing on the class index (option B) wrongly implies that category 11 is "closer" to 12 than to 1.

questions.q: A data scientist standardizes all features using the mean and standard deviation of the full dataset and then splits it into train and test sets. What is wrong?
options: Standardization should only be applied to the target
Nothing is wrong as long as the split is random
Test-set statistics leak into training, inflating evaluation results
Standardization makes the model unable to converge
questions.why: Preprocessing statistics must be fit on the training split only and then applied to validation and test data. Fitting on the full dataset lets information from the test set influence training, which a random split does not prevent.

questions.q: What does L2 regularization add to the training loss?
options: The sum of absolute values of the weights
The sum of squared weights, scaled by a coefficient
Random noise added to the input features
The number of non-zero weights
questions.why: L2 (ridge, weight decay) penalizes λΣw², pushing weights toward small values without making them exactly zero. The sum of absolute values (option A) is L1 regularization.

questions.q: A model has 5,000 input features and the team wants regularization that also drives many weights to exactly zero. Which should they use?
options: L1 regularization (Lasso)
L2 regularization (Ridge)
Dropout
Batch normalization
questions.why: The L1 penalty has a constant-magnitude gradient that can push weights all the way to zero, producing sparse models that act as built-in feature selection. L2 shrinks weights toward zero but rarely makes them exactly zero.

questions.q: How does dropout regularize a neural network?
options: It removes the least important features from the dataset before training
It permanently deletes neurons with small weights after training
It lowers the learning rate when validation loss stalls
It randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training only
questions.why: Dropout randomly disables units on each training step so the network cannot rely on specific co-adapted neurons; at inference all units are used. Permanently removing small-weight neurons (option B) describes pruning, a compression technique.

questions.q: What does early stopping do?
options: Stops training when the training loss reaches zero
Stops each epoch after a fixed number of batches
Halts training when validation performance stops improving and keeps the best checkpoint
Stops gradient flow to the early layers of the network
questions.why: Early stopping monitors a validation metric, typically with a patience window, and restores the best weights, preventing the model from continuing into overfitting. Waiting for zero training loss (option A) would encourage memorization.

questions.q: After z-score standardization, what are the mean and standard deviation of a feature in the training set?
options: Mean 0.5, standard deviation 0.5
Mean 0, standard deviation 1
Minimum 0, maximum 1
Mean 1, standard deviation 0
questions.why: Standardization computes (x − μ)/σ, producing zero mean and unit variance. A [0, 1] range (option C) is the result of min-max normalization, a different scaling method.

questions.q: A feature "payment_method" has values {card, cash, transfer} with no natural order. How should it be encoded for a linear model?
options: One-hot encoding
Label encoding as 0, 1, 2
Min-max scaling
Log transform
questions.why: One-hot encoding creates a separate binary column per category, so the model does not assume any ordering. Integer label encoding imposes a false order and spacing (transfer = 2 × cash), which a linear model would take literally.

questions.q: Which statement best describes mini-batch gradient descent?
options: It computes the gradient over the entire dataset before each update
It updates weights once per epoch using a single random example
It avoids computing gradients by using random search
It updates weights using gradients averaged over a small subset of examples
questions.why: Mini-batch GD balances the stable but expensive full-batch gradient (option A) and the noisy single-example SGD update. It also maps well to GPUs, which process a batch of examples in parallel.

questions.q: What does backpropagation compute?
options: The optimal learning rate for each layer
The forward-pass activations for a batch
The gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter, using the chain rule
The updated weights directly, without an optimizer
questions.why: Backprop propagates error derivatives from the output back through each layer via the chain rule, efficiently producing all parameter gradients. It does not itself update weights; the optimizer (SGD, Adam, etc.) uses those gradients to do that.

questions.q: Why do neural networks need non-linear activation functions such as ReLU between layers?
options: To keep all activations between 0 and 1
Without them, stacked linear layers collapse to a single linear transformation
To reduce the number of parameters in each layer
To make the loss function convex
questions.why: A composition of linear maps is still linear, so depth adds no expressive power without non-linearities. ReLU (max(0, x)) is unbounded above, so option A is false for it; that property belongs to the sigmoid.

questions.q: A binary classifier ends with a single sigmoid unit. What is the range of its output?
options: Between 0 and 1
Between −1 and 1
Between 0 and +∞
Any real number
questions.why: The sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^(−z)) squashes any real input into (0, 1), so it can be read as the probability of the positive class. The range −1 to 1 (option B) belongs to tanh.

questions.q: What property does the output of a softmax layer always have?
options: Exactly one element equals 1 and the rest are 0
Each element is between −1 and 1
All elements are positive and sum to 1
Elements are sorted in descending order
questions.why: Softmax exponentiates each logit and divides by the sum, yielding a probability distribution over classes. A single 1 with zeros elsewhere (option A) is a one-hot vector, which is what argmax produces, not softmax.

questions.topic: Parameter count of a linear layer
questions.q: How many trainable parameters does `torch.nn.Linear(512, 256)` have (bias enabled)?
questions.why: The weight matrix has 512 × 256 = 131,072 entries plus one bias per output unit (256), giving 131,328. Option A forgets the bias, and option C adds 512 biases (one per input) instead of one per output.

questions.q: A spam filter produces TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 130. What is its precision?
questions.why: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 40 / 50 = 0.80: of the emails flagged as spam, 80% really were. Option A (40/60) is recall, which uses false negatives instead of false positives.

questions.q: A fraud model has TP = 45, FN = 15, FP = 5. What is its recall?
questions.why: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 45 / 60 = 0.75: the model catches 75% of actual fraud. The value 0.90 (45/50) is precision, a frequent mix-up.

questions.q: In a dataset where 99% of transactions are legitimate, a model that always predicts "legitimate" achieves 99% accuracy. What does this show?
options: The model is production-ready
The dataset should be shuffled again
Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data; precision, recall or F1 are more informative
The model is overfitting to the minority class
questions.why: The trivial majority-class predictor catches zero fraud yet scores 99% accuracy. Metrics focused on the positive class, such as recall and F1, expose that failure; the model is ignoring the minority class, not overfitting to it.

questions.q: How is the F1 score defined?
options: The arithmetic mean of precision and recall
The geometric mean of sensitivity and specificity
The product of precision and recall
The harmonic mean of precision and recall
questions.why: F1 = 2PR/(P + R). The harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller value, so a model cannot get a high F1 by excelling at only one of precision or recall, which the arithmetic mean (option A) would allow.

questions.q: For an early cancer-screening model whose positives are followed by a cheap confirmatory test, which error should the team most want to minimize?
options: False positives
False negatives
True negatives
Training loss
questions.why: Missing a real cancer case is far costlier than an extra confirmatory test, so the model should be tuned for high recall (few false negatives). Minimizing false positives would be the priority when each positive triggers an expensive or harmful action.

questions.q: Which statement about k-means clustering is correct?
options: The number of clusters k must be chosen before running the algorithm
It requires labeled training data
It always finds the globally optimal clustering
It builds a tree of nested clusters
questions.why: k-means alternates between assigning points to the nearest centroid and recomputing centroids, with k fixed in advance. It converges to a local optimum that depends on initialization, so option C is false; nested trees describe hierarchical clustering.

questions.q: What does principal component analysis (PCA) do?
options: Selects the original features most correlated with the label
Clusters samples into k groups
Projects data onto orthogonal directions that capture the most variance
Trains a classifier with a maximum-margin boundary
questions.why: PCA is an unsupervised linear dimensionality-reduction method that creates new features (principal components) as combinations of the originals. It does not use labels, so it is not supervised feature selection as in option A.

questions.q: How does a k-nearest neighbors (kNN) classifier make a prediction?
options: By evaluating a learned weight vector against the input
By following a sequence of if-else splits learned during training
By sampling from a learned probability distribution
By majority vote among the k closest training examples
questions.why: kNN is a "lazy" learner: it stores the training data and does the work at prediction time by finding the nearest points under a distance metric. It learns no weight vector (option A), which is why inference cost grows with dataset size.

questions.q: Which criterion is commonly used to choose splits in a classification decision tree?
options: Mean squared error of the predicted class index
Gini impurity or information gain (entropy)
Cosine similarity between features
Learning rate decay
questions.why: Classification trees pick the split that makes child nodes most "pure", measured by Gini impurity or the drop in entropy. Variance/MSE reduction is the criterion for regression trees, and it is applied to the target value, not a class index.

questions.q: What makes a random forest different from a single decision tree?
options: It averages many trees trained on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets
It trains trees sequentially, each correcting the previous one's errors
It uses a single very deep tree with pruning
It replaces splits with neural network layers
questions.why: Random forests use bagging plus feature randomness to build decorrelated trees whose votes are averaged. Sequential error correction (option B) describes gradient boosting, the other main tree-ensemble family.

questions.q: How does gradient boosting (e.g., XGBoost) build its ensemble?
options: Trains all trees independently in parallel and takes a majority vote
Fits one deep tree and prunes it back
Adds trees sequentially, each fit to the errors (gradients) of the current ensemble
Clusters the data and trains one tree per cluster
questions.why: Each new shallow tree approximates the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions, so the ensemble improves step by step. Independent parallel trees with voting (option A) is bagging/random forest.

questions.q: Despite its name, what task is logistic regression used for?
options: Predicting continuous values
Clustering
Dimensionality reduction
Classification
questions.why: Logistic regression models the probability of a class by passing a linear combination of features through the sigmoid, then thresholds it for a decision. "Regression" in the name refers to regressing the log-odds, not to predicting continuous targets.

questions.q: What does a linear support vector machine (SVM) optimize for when separating two classes?
options: The minimum number of misclassified training points, ignoring distance
The widest margin between the decision boundary and the nearest points of each class
The boundary passing through the class means
The highest likelihood of the data under a Gaussian model
questions.why: SVMs choose the maximum-margin hyperplane; the closest training points that define it are the support vectors. Simply minimizing misclassifications (option A) ignores the margin and generalizes worse.

questions.q: What distinguishes a generative model from a discriminative model?
options: A generative model learns the data distribution P(x) or P(x, y); a discriminative model learns P(y | x) directly
A generative model only works on images; a discriminative model only works on text
A generative model needs no training data
A discriminative model can create new samples; a generative model can only classify
questions.why: Modeling how the data itself is distributed is what allows generative models to sample new examples. Option D swaps the roles: discriminative models only learn decision boundaries and cannot generate data.

questions.q: What are the two networks in a generative adversarial network (GAN)?
options: An encoder and a decoder
A teacher and a student
A generator and a discriminator
A policy and a value function
questions.why: The generator produces fake samples from noise and the discriminator tries to tell real from fake; they are trained against each other. Encoder-decoder (option A) describes autoencoders and VAEs.

questions.q: What does a variational autoencoder (VAE) learn?
options: A direct mapping from labels to images with no latent space
A discriminator that scores how real an image looks
A sequence of denoising steps from pure noise
An encoder to a probabilistic latent distribution and a decoder that reconstructs data from latent samples
questions.why: A VAE encodes each input as a distribution (mean and variance) in latent space, samples from it, and decodes; new data is generated by decoding samples from the prior. Iterative denoising from noise (option C) is how diffusion models generate.

questions.q: How do diffusion models generate images?
options: By retrieving the nearest training image and editing it
By learning to reverse a gradual noising process, iteratively denoising random noise
By a single forward pass of a generator against a discriminator
By predicting image pixels with a decision tree
questions.why: Training corrupts data with increasing noise and teaches a network to remove it; sampling starts from pure noise and denoises over many steps. Single-pass generation with an adversary (option C) describes GANs.

questions.q: What is the core training objective of a GPT-style autoregressive language model?
options: Predict the next token given all previous tokens
Classify whether two sentences are paraphrases
Reconstruct an image from a latent vector
Cluster documents by topic
questions.why: Autoregressive LMs factor the probability of a sequence into next-token predictions and generate text one token at a time. Paraphrase classification (option B) is a downstream discriminative task, not the pretraining objective.

questions.q: A data scientist trains XGBoost 2.x on a large tabular dataset and wants it to run on an NVIDIA GPU. What change is needed?
options: Rewrite the model in PyTorch
Convert the tabular rows to images first
Set the parameter device="cuda" with the hist tree method
Replace XGBoost with cuGraph
questions.why: XGBoost has native CUDA support; from version 2.0, device="cuda" with tree_method="hist" trains on the GPU (older versions used tree_method="gpu_hist"). cuGraph is the RAPIDS graph-analytics library and does not do gradient boosting.

questions.q: A data engineering team runs large Spark SQL and DataFrame ETL jobs and wants GPU acceleration with minimal code changes. Which option fits best?
options: cuML
TensorRT
Triton Inference Server
RAPIDS Accelerator for Apache Spark
questions.why: The RAPIDS Accelerator is a Spark plugin that runs supported SQL and DataFrame operations on GPUs, largely without changing job code. cuML provides GPU machine-learning algorithms, not a Spark execution engine.

questions.q: Which of the following is a hyperparameter rather than a learned parameter?
options: The weights of a linear layer
The learning rate
The bias terms of a neuron
The split thresholds learned inside a decision tree
questions.why: Hyperparameters are set before training and control how learning happens; the learning rate is a classic example. Weights, biases and learned split thresholds are all fitted from data during training.

questions.q: In 5-fold cross-validation, how is the model evaluated?
options: It is trained 5 times, each time validating on a different fold and training on the other 4, then the scores are averaged
It is trained once on 80% of the data and validated 5 times on the same 20%
It is trained on 5 copies of the full dataset
It is evaluated on the training data 5 times with different seeds
questions.why: Every example is used for validation exactly once, giving a more reliable estimate than a single split, especially on small datasets. Validating repeatedly on the same 20% (option B) gains nothing over a single hold-out split.

questions.q: A model with high bias and low variance typically shows which behavior?
options: Very low training error and high test error
Predictions that change drastically with small changes to the training set
High training error and similar test error (underfitting)
Perfect memorization of training data
questions.why: High bias means overly simple assumptions, so the model misses patterns even on training data, while low variance means its predictions are stable across datasets. Options A and B describe high variance (overfitting).

questions.q: What is a key advantage of deep learning over classical ML on unstructured data such as images, audio and text?
options: It needs far less training data
It is always easier to interpret
It trains faster on CPUs
It learns useful feature representations directly from raw data
questions.why: Deep networks learn hierarchical features automatically instead of relying on hand-engineered ones, which is why they dominate unstructured data. They usually need more data and compute (typically GPUs), not less, so option A is the opposite of the truth.

questions.q: A churn model reaches 99% validation accuracy. One feature is "account_closed_date", which is filled in only after a customer churns. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The model has learned genuinely strong churn signals
Target leakage from a feature that is not available at prediction time
The validation set is too large
The model is underfitting
questions.why: The feature encodes the outcome itself and would not exist when predicting future churn, so the score is unrealistically high and will collapse in production. Suspiciously near-perfect validation scores are a classic leakage symptom, not evidence of a strong model.

questions.q: An engineer is building a model to forecast next week's demand from three years of daily sales. How should the data be split for validation?
options: Random 80/20 shuffle split
Stratified split by product category
Leave-one-out cross-validation over random days
Train on earlier periods and validate on later periods
questions.why: Forecasting must be evaluated the way it is used: predicting the future from the past. A random shuffle lets the model train on days after the ones it is validated on, leaking future information and overstating accuracy.

questions.q: A medical dataset has only 3% positive cases. A random split leaves the validation set with almost no positives. What should the team use?
options: A stratified split that preserves the class ratio in each subset
A larger batch size
Min-max scaling of the labels
A time-based split
questions.why: Stratification ensures each split (and each CV fold) contains roughly 3% positives, so validation metrics for the rare class are meaningful. A time-based split addresses temporal leakage, not class proportion.

questions.q: A fraud classifier trained on 1% fraud cases predicts almost everything as legitimate. Which change most directly addresses this?
options: Increase the number of hidden layers
Remove the minority class from validation
Apply class weights in the loss or oversample the minority class
Switch the loss to mean squared error
questions.why: Weighting the minority class (or resampling, e.g., SMOTE or undersampling the majority) makes mistakes on fraud cost more during training. Adding capacity does not change the fact that the loss is dominated by the majority class.

questions.q: A binary classifier uses a 0.5 probability threshold. The team lowers the threshold to 0.3. What typically happens?
options: Precision rises and recall falls
Recall rises and precision falls
Both precision and recall rise
The ROC-AUC changes
questions.why: A lower threshold labels more examples positive, catching more true positives but also admitting more false positives. ROC-AUC is threshold-independent because it summarizes performance across all thresholds, so it does not change.

questions.q: A model has ROC-AUC = 0.85. What does this mean?
options: 85% of predictions are correct
Precision is 0.85 at the default threshold
The model misclassifies 15% of positives
A randomly chosen positive is ranked above a randomly chosen negative 85% of the time
questions.why: AUC measures ranking quality across all thresholds; 0.5 is random and 1.0 is perfect separation. It is not accuracy (option A), which depends on a single threshold and the class balance.

questions.q: For a highly imbalanced problem (0.1% positives) where the positive class matters most, which evaluation curve is usually more informative?
options: Precision-recall curve
ROC curve
Training loss curve
Learning-rate finder curve
questions.why: With a huge negative class, the false positive rate on the ROC curve stays tiny even when false positives vastly outnumber true positives, so ROC can look optimistic. Precision directly reflects that flood of false positives, making the PR curve more revealing.

questions.q: Which learning-rate schedule is widely used when training large neural networks from scratch?
options: A constant high learning rate throughout
Increasing the learning rate steadily until the end of training
A short linear warmup followed by cosine or linear decay
Randomly sampling a new learning rate every step
questions.why: Warmup avoids unstable large updates while the weights and optimizer statistics are still poorly calibrated, and decay lets the model settle into a minimum. A constant high learning rate keeps bouncing around the minimum late in training.

questions.q: What problem does adding momentum to SGD mainly address?
options: It removes the need for a learning rate
It dampens oscillations and speeds progress along consistent gradient directions
It prevents overfitting by adding noise to the weights
It normalizes each layer's activations
questions.why: Momentum keeps an exponentially decaying average of past gradients (a "velocity"), so components that flip sign cancel out and consistent ones accumulate. It still needs a learning rate; it is an optimization aid rather than a regularizer.

questions.q: What distinguishes the Adam optimizer from plain SGD?
options: It computes exact second derivatives (the Hessian)
It uses a single global learning rate with no gradient history
It only works for convex losses
It adapts per-parameter step sizes using running averages of the gradient and squared gradient
questions.why: Adam combines momentum (first moment) with RMSProp-style scaling (second moment), so each parameter gets its own effective learning rate. The squared-gradient average is a cheap diagonal approximation, not the full Hessian.

questions.q: What is the key change in AdamW compared with Adam plus an L2 penalty?
options: Weight decay is decoupled from the adaptive gradient update and applied directly to the weights
It removes the first-moment (momentum) estimate
It uses a fixed learning rate that cannot be scheduled
It applies dropout to the optimizer states
questions.why: In Adam with L2, the penalty's gradient is divided by the adaptive denominator, weakening regularization for some weights. AdamW shrinks the weights separately, which tends to generalize better and is the default for training transformers.

questions.q: A 30-layer network with sigmoid activations barely updates its early layers. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Replace the loss with MSE
Increase the batch size tenfold
Use ReLU-family activations and residual connections
Remove the bias terms
questions.why: The sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25, so multiplying it across many layers shrinks gradients toward zero. ReLU has derivative 1 for positive inputs, and residual connections give gradients a direct path to early layers; batch size does not change this multiplicative effect.

questions.q: Gradient norms in an RNN occasionally spike by several orders of magnitude, causing the loss to jump to NaN. Which technique directly addresses this?
options: Early stopping
Gradient clipping
L1 regularization
One-hot encoding the inputs
questions.why: Clipping rescales gradients whose norm exceeds a threshold, preventing a single huge update from destroying the weights. Early stopping only decides when to end training; it does nothing to stop a spike mid-run.

questions.q: What does batch normalization do during training?
options: Normalizes the input dataset once before training
Scales gradients so their norm stays below a threshold
Divides the learning rate by the batch size
Normalizes a layer's activations using the mean and variance of the current mini-batch, then applies a learned scale and shift
questions.why: BatchNorm stabilizes and speeds up training by keeping intermediate activations well-scaled. At inference it uses running averages collected during training, not batch statistics; normalizing raw inputs once (option A) is ordinary preprocessing.

questions.q:
```python
for x, y in loader:
    loss = criterion(model(x), y)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
```

Training becomes unstable after a few steps. What is missing?
options: `optimizer.zero_grad()` before `loss.backward()`
`model.eval()` before the forward pass
`torch.no_grad()` around `optimizer.step()`
`loss.item()` before `backward()`
questions.why: PyTorch accumulates gradients in `.grad` by default, so without zeroing them each step adds the new gradient to all previous ones, producing ever-larger updates. Calling `model.eval()` during training would disable dropout and change BatchNorm behavior, which is wrong here.

questions.q: A model with dropout and BatchNorm gives slightly different predictions each time it is run on the same input at inference. What call was most likely forgotten?
options: `optimizer.zero_grad()`
`model.train()`
`model.eval()`
`torch.manual_seed()` before training
questions.why: `model.eval()` switches dropout off and makes BatchNorm use its running statistics, giving deterministic predictions. `model.train()` is the default mode that causes the randomness; setting a seed would only hide the symptom.

questions.q: Why wrap inference code in `with torch.no_grad():`?
options: It switches dropout off
It stops autograd from recording operations, saving memory and compute
It freezes BatchNorm running statistics
It converts the model to FP16
questions.why: Without gradient tracking, PyTorch does not keep intermediate activations for backprop, so inference is lighter and faster. It does not change layer behavior; dropout and BatchNorm modes are controlled by `model.eval()`.

questions.q: Validation loss reaches its minimum at epoch 8 and rises steadily through epoch 20, while training loss keeps falling. With early stopping (patience = 3), which checkpoint should be kept?
options: Epoch 20
Epoch 11
Epoch 1
Epoch 8
questions.why: Early stopping halts training after 3 epochs without improvement (epoch 11) but restores the checkpoint with the best validation loss, epoch 8. Keeping epoch 11 would retain three epochs of overfitting.

questions.q: A 10-class classifier's cross-entropy loss stays at about 2.30 from the first step and never decreases. What does this indicate?
options: The model is predicting a near-uniform distribution over the 10 classes
The model has converged to a perfect solution
The model is confidently predicting the wrong class
The dataset has only two classes
questions.why: −ln(1/10) ≈ 2.30, which is exactly the loss of assigning 0.1 to every class, so the model is not learning (check learning rate, labels and gradient flow). Confidently wrong predictions would push the loss well above 2.30.

questions.q: For one example, a classifier assigns probability 0.25 to the correct class. What is the cross-entropy loss (natural log)?
questions.why: Cross-entropy for a single example is −ln(p_correct) = −ln(0.25) ≈ 1.386. The value 2.00 is −log₂(0.25), which would be the answer in bits rather than nats.

questions.q: Two-class logits are [0, ln 3]. What probability does softmax assign to the second class?
questions.why: softmax gives e^(ln 3) / (e⁰ + e^(ln 3)) = 3 / (1 + 3) = 0.75. Option A would be correct only if the two logits were equal; exponentiation turns a logit gap of ln 3 into a 3:1 probability ratio.

questions.q: What is the dot product of vectors [1, 2, 3] and [4, −1, 2]?
questions.why: 1×4 + 2×(−1) + 3×2 = 4 − 2 + 6 = 8. The value 12 results from ignoring the minus sign on the second component.

questions.q: A batch of activations X has shape (32, 128) and a weight matrix W has shape (128, 64). What is the shape of X @ W?
options: The product is undefined
questions.why: For (m, n) @ (n, p) the inner dimensions must match and the result is (m, p): 32 examples each mapped to 64 features. Option C would be the transpose, (W^T X^T).

questions.q: What is the Shannon entropy of a fair coin flip, in bits?
questions.why: H = −Σ p log₂ p = −2 × 0.5 × log₂(0.5) = 1 bit, the maximum for two outcomes. Entropy is 0 only for a certain outcome, such as a coin that always lands heads.

questions.q: Which statement about the Kullback–Leibler divergence KL(P‖Q) is correct?
options: It is symmetric: KL(P‖Q) = KL(Q‖P)
It is non-negative and equals zero only when P and Q are identical
It can be negative when Q is broader than P
It is a true distance metric satisfying the triangle inequality
questions.why: KL divergence measures how much information is lost when Q approximates P, and Gibbs' inequality guarantees it is ≥ 0. It is asymmetric and violates the triangle inequality, so it is a divergence rather than a metric.

questions.q: Why do ML systems usually work with log-probabilities instead of multiplying raw probabilities across many terms?
options: Log-probabilities are always positive
Logs make probabilities sum to 1
Logs remove the need for normalization
Products of many small probabilities underflow, while sums of logs stay numerically stable
questions.why: Multiplying hundreds of values below 1 quickly rounds to zero in floating point; log turns the product into a sum that stays representable. Log-probabilities are ≤ 0, not positive, so option A is false.

questions.q: Which algorithm is least affected by whether features are standardized?
options: Random forest
k-nearest neighbors
Support vector machine with RBF kernel
k-means
questions.why: Tree splits compare a single feature to a threshold, so monotonic rescaling does not change which splits are possible. kNN, k-means and RBF SVMs rely on distances, where a feature measured in large units would dominate unless features are scaled.

questions.q: A feature ranges from 10 to 60 in the training set. Using min-max scaling to [0, 1], what is the scaled value of 30?
questions.why: (x − min)/(max − min) = (30 − 10)/(60 − 10) = 20/50 = 0.40. Option D (30/50) forgets to subtract the minimum from the numerator.

questions.q: A numeric "income" feature has missing values and a few extreme outliers. Which simple imputation is most robust?
options: Mean imputation
Median imputation
Replacing missing values with 0
Replacing missing values with the maximum
questions.why: The median is not pulled by extreme values, so it gives a representative fill-in for skewed data like income. The mean can be dragged far upward by a few billionaires, and zero introduces an artificial cluster of fake values.

questions.q: A kNN classifier works well with 10 features but degrades badly after adding 2,000 sparse features. What is the most likely reason?
options: kNN cannot handle numeric features
The learning rate is too high
The model is underfitting due to too few parameters
In high dimensions, distances between points become nearly uniform, so "nearest" neighbors are not meaningfully close
questions.why: As dimensionality grows, data becomes sparse and the gap between nearest and farthest neighbors shrinks, undermining distance-based methods. kNN has no learning rate, so option B does not apply; dimensionality reduction or feature selection is the usual fix.

questions.q: A data scientist plots within-cluster sum of squares against k for k-means and looks for the point where improvement sharply flattens. What is this technique called?
options: The elbow method
Grid search over learning rates
Bootstrap aggregation
Cross-entropy minimization
questions.why: Inertia always decreases as k grows, so the "elbow" where extra clusters stop giving large gains is a common heuristic for k. Silhouette scores are another option; grid search over learning rates is unrelated since k-means has no learning rate.

questions.q: After PCA on 200 features, the first 20 components explain 95% of the variance. What is a reasonable use of this result?
options: Drop the 20 components and keep the remaining 180
Conclude that the 20 original features with the highest variance are the only useful ones
Keep the first 20 components as a compressed representation that retains most of the information
Conclude that the label depends on only 20 features
questions.why: Components are ordered by explained variance, so keeping the top 20 reduces dimensionality tenfold while preserving 95% of variance. Components are combinations of all original features, not a subset of them (option B), and PCA ignores the label entirely.

questions.q: A single deep decision tree has 100% training accuracy but unstable, poor validation accuracy. Why does switching to a random forest usually help?
options: It lowers bias by making each tree deeper
Averaging many decorrelated trees reduces variance
It converts the problem into regression
It removes the need for training data
questions.why: A deep tree has low bias but high variance; averaging many trees built on different bootstrap samples and feature subsets cancels out much of that variance. Bias stays roughly the same as an individual tree, so option A misstates the mechanism.

questions.q: A team has a structured tabular dataset of 500,000 rows with mixed numeric and categorical features. Which model family is typically the strongest first baseline?
options: A large diffusion model
k-means clustering
An autoregressive language model
Gradient-boosted decision trees such as XGBoost
questions.why: Boosted trees handle heterogeneous features, missing values and non-linear interactions well and routinely win on tabular benchmarks; XGBoost can also train on GPUs. k-means is unsupervised and cannot be used directly for a labeled prediction task.

questions.q: In logistic regression, what quantity is modeled as a linear function of the features?
options: The log-odds of the positive class
The class probability directly
The squared error
The class label 0 or 1
questions.why: Logistic regression assumes log(p/(1−p)) = w·x + b and recovers p with the sigmoid. Modeling the probability directly as linear (option B) could produce values outside [0, 1], which is exactly what the logit link avoids.

questions.q: Ordinary least squares linear regression has a closed-form solution. Which is it?
options: w = X^T y
w = (X X^T)⁻¹ y
w = (X^T X)⁻¹ X^T y
w = X⁻¹ y
questions.why: The normal equation sets the gradient of the squared error to zero. X is usually not square, so it has no ordinary inverse (option D); X^T X is the square matrix that gets inverted.

questions.q: A kNN classifier with k = 1 has perfect training accuracy but noisy validation results. What does increasing k generally do?
options: Increases variance and makes the decision boundary more jagged
Smooths the decision boundary, reducing variance at the cost of more bias
Has no effect on predictions
Makes training slower but inference faster
questions.why: With k = 1 each prediction copies a single, possibly noisy, neighbor; voting over more neighbors averages out noise. Too large a k oversmooths and underfits, so k is tuned on validation data.

questions.q: What does the kernel trick allow an SVM to do?
options: Train without any labeled examples
Use gradient boosting internally
Avoid choosing a regularization parameter
Learn non-linear decision boundaries by computing inner products in a higher-dimensional space implicitly
questions.why: Kernels such as RBF or polynomial compute similarity as if the data were mapped to a richer feature space, without ever constructing that space. The SVM still needs labels and its C regularization parameter.

questions.q: A regression problem has many highly correlated features, and the team wants both sparsity and stable coefficient estimates. Which regularization fits best?
options: Elastic Net (combined L1 and L2)
Pure L1 (Lasso)
No regularization
Dropout
questions.why: Lasso alone tends to pick one feature from a correlated group arbitrarily and can be unstable; adding an L2 term spreads weight across correlated features while L1 still zeroes irrelevant ones. Dropout is a neural-network technique and does not produce sparse linear coefficients.

questions.q: What happens as the regularization coefficient λ is increased substantially?
options: Variance increases and bias decreases
Training error decreases
Bias increases and variance decreases
The model gains more effective capacity
questions.why: A stronger penalty constrains the weights, simplifying the model: less sensitivity to the training set (lower variance) but more systematic error (higher bias). Training error generally rises with heavier regularization, not falls.

questions.q: What is leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) equivalent to?
options: A single 50/50 train/validation split
k-fold cross-validation with k equal to the number of examples
Bootstrap sampling with replacement
2-fold cross-validation repeated n times
questions.why: Each model is trained on n − 1 examples and validated on the single held-out one, repeated n times. It makes maximal use of small datasets but is expensive, requiring n training runs.

questions.q: A model predicts disease from X-ray images, with several images per patient. A random image-level split gives excellent results that do not hold up on new patients. What split should have been used?
options: A stratified split by image brightness
A larger random test set
A time-based split by image file name
A group-based split so that all images of a patient fall in the same subset
questions.why: With images of the same patient in both train and test, the model can recognize patient-specific features instead of disease signs. Grouping by patient (e.g., scikit-learn's GroupKFold) measures generalization to unseen patients; a larger random split would leak in the same way.

questions.q: When only a few of many hyperparameters strongly affect performance, why is random search often more efficient than grid search for the same budget?
options: It tries more distinct values of each important hyperparameter
It always finds the global optimum
It needs no validation set
It evaluates every combination exhaustively
questions.why: A 5×5 grid tests only 5 values of each hyperparameter, while 25 random trials test up to 25 distinct values of each, so the important dimensions get explored better. Neither method guarantees a global optimum, and both need validation data.

questions.q: A team increases the batch size from 64 to 1,024 on the same dataset and number of epochs. Which outcome is expected?
options: More optimizer steps per epoch
Lower GPU memory usage
Fewer optimizer steps per epoch, with a larger learning rate often needed
No change in gradient noise
questions.why: A 16× larger batch means 16× fewer updates per epoch and less noisy gradients, so the learning rate is commonly scaled up (with warmup) to compensate. It also requires more activation memory, not less.

questions.q: Training uses 2 GPUs, a per-GPU micro-batch of 8, and 4 gradient-accumulation steps. What is the effective global batch size?
questions.why: Effective batch = micro-batch × accumulation steps × data-parallel GPUs = 8 × 4 × 2 = 64. Gradient accumulation sums gradients over several forward/backward passes before one optimizer step, letting a large batch fit in limited memory; option C forgets the second GPU.

questions.q: What does mixed-precision training on NVIDIA GPUs typically involve?
options: Training entirely in INT8 including gradients
Alternating between CPU and GPU each step
Using FP64 for activations and FP32 for weights
Computing most operations in FP16/BF16 while keeping an FP32 master copy of the weights
questions.why: Half-precision math runs on Tensor Cores with less memory traffic, while FP32 master weights preserve small updates; with FP16, loss scaling prevents gradient underflow. INT8 is mainly an inference quantization format, not a standard training precision.

questions.q: Why is BF16 often preferred over FP16 for training large models?
options: It has the same exponent range as FP32, so overflow/underflow and loss scaling are less of a concern
It has more mantissa bits than FP16, giving higher precision
It uses half the memory of FP16
It is supported on CPUs only
questions.why: BF16 keeps FP32's 8 exponent bits but only 7 mantissa bits, trading precision for range. FP16 has more mantissa bits (10), so option B has it backwards; both are 16-bit formats with equal memory.

questions.q: All weights in a multilayer perceptron are initialized to zero. What happens during training?
options: Training converges faster because all weights start equal
Gradients explode immediately
Neurons in the same layer receive identical updates and never learn different features
The network automatically switches to random initialization
questions.why: Identical weights produce identical outputs and gradients, so the symmetry is never broken and a layer behaves like a single neuron. Random initialization (e.g., Xavier or He) is required; zero weights tend to give zero or tiny gradients, not explosions.

questions.q: A data scientist has a large existing pandas workflow and wants GPU acceleration with no code changes, falling back to CPU for unsupported operations. What should they use?
options: Rewrite it with cuML estimators
The cudf.pandas accelerator mode
TensorRT
Convert the DataFrame to a PyTorch tensor
questions.why: Loading `cudf.pandas` (e.g., `%load_ext cudf.pandas` in Jupyter or `python -m cudf.pandas script.py`) runs pandas operations on the GPU via cuDF and transparently falls back to pandas on the CPU when needed. cuML accelerates ML algorithms, not DataFrame manipulation.

questions.q: In which situation is moving a classical ML workflow to RAPIDS on a GPU least likely to pay off?
options: Training random forests on 50 million rows
Running k-means repeatedly on a large dataset during tuning
Joining and aggregating multi-gigabyte tables
A one-off model on a 2,000-row CSV
questions.why: GPU acceleration shines when there is enough parallel work to amortize data transfer and kernel-launch overhead; tiny datasets already run in milliseconds on a CPU. Large training, repeated tuning and big joins are exactly where cuDF and cuML give large speedups.

questions.q: A cuDF workflow no longer fits in a single GPU's memory. Which approach lets the team distribute the DataFrame across multiple GPUs?
options: Dask with dask-cudf
Increasing the batch size
Converting the data to JSON
Using scikit-learn instead
questions.why: Dask partitions a large DataFrame into many cuDF partitions spread across GPUs (and nodes), scheduling work in parallel. scikit-learn is CPU-only and single-node, so it would be a step backwards for this workload.

questions.q: A GAN trained on handwritten digits produces sharp images, but almost all of them are the digit "1". What is this failure called?
options: Overfitting of the discriminator to noise
Vanishing gradient in the encoder
Mode collapse
Posterior collapse
questions.why: In mode collapse the generator finds a few outputs that fool the discriminator and stops covering the diversity of the data. Posterior collapse is a VAE failure where the decoder ignores the latent code.

questions.q: What are the two terms in a standard VAE training objective?
options: Adversarial loss and cycle-consistency loss
Reconstruction loss and a KL divergence between the latent distribution and a prior
Hinge loss and L1 penalty
Next-token loss and contrastive loss
questions.why: The reconstruction term makes decoded outputs match the inputs, and the KL term keeps the encoder's distributions close to a simple prior (usually a standard Gaussian), so sampling from that prior produces valid data. Adversarial plus cycle-consistency losses belong to CycleGAN.

questions.q: Why do latent diffusion models (such as Stable Diffusion) run the diffusion process in a compressed latent space rather than in pixel space?
options: Pixel-space diffusion cannot generate color images
Latent space removes the need for any denoising steps
It allows the model to skip training entirely
It greatly reduces compute per denoising step while an autoencoder handles pixel detail
questions.why: An autoencoder compresses images into a much smaller latent tensor; the diffusion model denoises there, and the decoder maps the result back to pixels. Sampling still takes multiple denoising steps; they are just much cheaper.

questions.q: How does an autoregressive model factor the probability of a sequence x₁…x_T?
options: p(x) = Π_t p(x_t | x₁, …, x_{t−1})
p(x) = Π_t p(x_t), assuming independence
p(x) = p(x_T | x₁)
p(x) = Σ_t p(x_t | x_{t+1})
questions.why: The chain rule of probability expresses the joint distribution exactly as a product of next-element conditionals, which is what the model learns. Assuming independence (option B) would discard all dependence between tokens.

questions.q: Which of these classifiers is a generative model?
options: Logistic regression
Linear SVM
Naive Bayes
A decision tree
questions.why: Naive Bayes models P(x | y) and P(y) and applies Bayes' rule to classify, so it models how features are generated per class. Logistic regression models P(y | x) directly, making it the textbook discriminative counterpart.

questions.q: A disease has 1% prevalence. A test has 90% sensitivity and a 9% false positive rate. Roughly what is the probability that a person who tests positive has the disease?
questions.why: P(D | +) = (0.01 × 0.90) / (0.01 × 0.90 + 0.99 × 0.09) = 0.009 / 0.0981 ≈ 9%. Answering 90% confuses P(+ | D) with P(D | +), ignoring the low base rate.

questions.q: A team has only 800 labeled images for a new defect-detection task. Which approach is most likely to give good accuracy?
options: Training a large CNN from random initialization
k-means on raw pixel values
Increasing the number of epochs to 1,000
Starting from a model pretrained on a large image dataset and adapting it to the new task
questions.why: Transfer learning reuses general features (edges, textures, shapes) learned from large data, so the small labeled set only has to teach task-specific distinctions. Training from scratch on 800 images with many more epochs would mostly memorize them.

questions.q: A regression dataset contains occasional large outliers caused by sensor glitches. Which loss is less sensitive to them than MSE?
options: Mean absolute error or Huber loss
Squared hinge loss
Root mean squared error
Categorical cross-entropy
questions.why: MSE squares residuals, so a single large outlier dominates the gradient; MAE grows linearly, and Huber is quadratic near zero but linear for large errors. Cross-entropy is a classification loss and does not apply to continuous targets.

questions.q: Each news article can have several tags simultaneously (e.g., "politics" and "economy"). How should the output layer and loss be set up?
options: Softmax over tags with categorical cross-entropy
A single linear output with MSE
An independent sigmoid per tag with binary cross-entropy
Argmax over tags with hinge loss
questions.why: Multi-label problems treat each tag as its own yes/no decision, so each output gets a sigmoid and a binary loss. Softmax forces probabilities to sum to 1, which makes tags compete as if only one could be correct.

questions.q: Adam initializes its first-moment estimate m₀ = 0 with β₁ = 0.9. After the first step, m₁ = 0.1·g₁. What does bias correction compute, and why?
options: m̂₁ = 0.9·m₁, to slow down early updates
m̂₁ = m₁ / (1 − 0.9¹) = g₁, to undo the bias toward zero from the zero initialization
m̂₁ = m₁ / (1 + 0.9), to normalize by the momentum sum
No correction is applied; the small early steps act as warmup by design
questions.why: Because the moving averages start at zero, early estimates are shrunk toward zero; dividing by (1 − β^t) rescales them to unbiased estimates, with the effect vanishing as t grows. Adam does apply this correction, so relying on it as implicit warmup (option D) is incorrect, which is partly why explicit warmup is still used.

questions.topic: L2 penalty vs decoupled weight decay
questions.q: Why is adding an L2 penalty to the loss not equivalent to weight decay when using Adam?
options: Adam ignores any term added to the loss
L2 penalties only apply to bias terms in Adam
They are equivalent; AdamW only changes the default hyperparameters
The penalty's gradient is divided by Adam's per-parameter second-moment term, so weights with large historic gradients are decayed less
questions.why: With plain SGD, L2 regularization and weight decay coincide up to a rescaling of λ, but adaptive scaling breaks that equivalence. AdamW applies θ ← θ − ηλθ separately from the adaptive step, restoring uniform decay; it is a different update rule, not just new defaults.

questions.q: As model size grows past the point where it can exactly fit the training data, test error rises and then falls again. What is this phenomenon called?
options: Double descent
Catastrophic forgetting
Grokking-induced underfitting
The vanishing gradient problem
questions.why: Double descent describes a second decrease in test error beyond the interpolation threshold, contradicting the classical U-shaped bias-variance curve for heavily over-parameterized models. Catastrophic forgetting concerns losing old skills when training on new tasks, not a function of model size.

questions.q: Computing softmax on logits like [1000, 1001, 1002] in FP32 returns NaN. What is the standard fix?
options: Divide all logits by their sum before exponentiating
Clip logits to the range [0, 1]
Subtract the maximum logit from every logit before exponentiating
Use the absolute value of the logits
questions.why: Softmax is invariant to adding a constant to all logits, so subtracting the max gives [−2, −1, 0], which exponentiates safely without overflow. Clipping or dividing changes the relative logit gaps and therefore the resulting probabilities.

questions.q:
```python
logits = model(x)
probs = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
loss = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(probs, y)
```

The model trains very slowly and its predictions are poorly calibrated. What is the bug?
options: `dim=-1` should be `dim=0`
`CrossEntropyLoss` already applies log-softmax internally, so it should receive raw logits
`y` must be one-hot encoded for `CrossEntropyLoss`
`CrossEntropyLoss` requires probabilities, so a sigmoid should be used instead
questions.why: Passing probabilities applies softmax twice, squashing the inputs into [0, 1] so the loss surface is flattened and gradients are weak. PyTorch's `CrossEntropyLoss` accepts integer class indices for `y`, so one-hot encoding is not required.

questions.q: With label smoothing ε = 0.1 over K = 5 classes (target = (1 − ε)·one_hot + ε/K), what is the target probability for the correct class and for each other class?
questions.why: Each class receives ε/K = 0.02, and the true class also keeps 1 − ε = 0.90, for 0.92 total; the five targets sum to 0.92 + 4 × 0.02 = 1. Option A spreads ε only over the K − 1 wrong classes, which is a different (also used) variant than the formula given.

questions.q: An object detector is overwhelmed by a huge number of easy background examples. What does focal loss do to address this?
options: Multiplies cross-entropy by (1 − p_t)^γ, down-weighting well-classified examples
Removes all negative examples from training
Replaces cross-entropy with MSE on probabilities
Increases the learning rate for the minority class only
questions.why: When the model already assigns high probability p_t to the true class, the modulating factor approaches zero, so training focuses on hard, misclassified examples. Discarding all negatives (option B) would make the detector unable to learn what background looks like.

questions.q: Why is layer normalization often preferred over batch normalization for sequence models and very small batches?
options: LayerNorm has no learnable parameters
LayerNorm normalizes across the batch dimension, giving more stable statistics
LayerNorm computes statistics per example across features, so it does not depend on batch size or other examples
BatchNorm cannot be used with ReLU activations
questions.why: BatchNorm statistics become noisy with tiny batches and are awkward with variable-length sequences, and train and inference behavior differ. LayerNorm still has a learnable scale and shift (so option A is false); it is BatchNorm that normalizes across the batch.

questions.q: PyTorch uses inverted dropout with drop probability p = 0.2. During training, what happens to the activations that are kept?
options: They are multiplied by 0.8
They are multiplied by 1.25
They are unchanged, and outputs are multiplied by 0.8 at inference
They are multiplied by 0.2
questions.why: Inverted dropout scales surviving activations by 1/(1 − p) = 1/0.8 = 1.25 during training so the expected activation is unchanged, letting inference run with no rescaling. Option C describes the original (non-inverted) formulation, not what PyTorch implements.

questions.q: Which weight initialization is designed to preserve activation variance in deep networks using ReLU?
options: Xavier/Glorot with variance 1/fan_avg
All weights set to 0.01
Orthogonal initialization of biases only
He (Kaiming) initialization with variance 2/fan_in
questions.why: ReLU zeroes roughly half of its inputs, halving the variance, so He initialization doubles the weight variance to compensate. Xavier initialization was derived for symmetric activations like tanh and tends to shrink signals in deep ReLU networks.

questions.q: A model's full gradient vector is [6, 8] and global-norm clipping uses max_norm = 1.0. What is the clipped gradient?
options: [6, 8], unchanged
questions.why: The norm is √(36 + 64) = 10 > 1, so every component is scaled by 1/10, preserving direction while capping magnitude. Option B is per-value clipping (clamping each element to 1), which changes the gradient's direction.

questions.q: When fitting a single Gaussian Q to a bimodal distribution P, how do the two KL directions behave?
options: Both directions give the same Q because KL is symmetric
Minimizing KL(Q‖P) spreads Q over both modes; KL(P‖Q) locks onto one mode
Minimizing KL(P‖Q) spreads Q to cover both modes; minimizing KL(Q‖P) tends to lock onto one mode
Neither can be minimized for multimodal P
questions.why: Forward KL heavily penalizes Q being near zero where P has mass (mode-covering), while reverse KL heavily penalizes Q putting mass where P is near zero (mode-seeking). Option B reverses the two behaviors, a very common mistake.

questions.q: For a fixed data distribution p and model q, how is cross-entropy H(p, q) related to KL divergence?
options: H(p, q) = KL(p‖q) − H(p)
H(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p‖q), so minimizing cross-entropy over q also minimizes KL
H(p, q) = KL(q‖p)
They are unrelated quantities
questions.why: The data entropy H(p) is constant with respect to the model, so the only part of the cross-entropy the model can reduce is the KL term. This is why training with cross-entropy is equivalent to making the model distribution match the data distribution.

questions.q: Minimizing mean squared error in regression is equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation under which assumption?
options: Laplace-distributed noise
Bernoulli-distributed targets
Uniform noise
Gaussian noise with constant variance
questions.why: The Gaussian log-likelihood is −(y − ŷ)²/(2σ²) plus a constant, so maximizing it is minimizing squared error. Laplace noise leads to mean absolute error instead, and Bernoulli targets lead to binary cross-entropy.

questions.q: From a Bayesian MAP perspective, which priors on the weights correspond to L2 and L1 regularization?
options: L2 ↔ Gaussian prior; L1 ↔ Laplace prior
L2 ↔ Laplace prior; L1 ↔ Gaussian prior
Both correspond to a uniform prior
L2 ↔ Bernoulli prior; L1 ↔ Poisson prior
questions.why: The negative log of a zero-mean Gaussian is proportional to w², and that of a Laplace density is proportional to |w|. The Laplace prior's sharp peak at zero is what drives L1 solutions to exact sparsity; option B swaps the pairing.

questions.q: Two features are perfectly collinear, so X^T X is singular and OLS has no unique solution. How does ridge regression fix this?
options: It drops one of the collinear features automatically
It uses the pseudo-inverse of X instead of X^T X
It solves (X^T X + λI)w = X^T y, and adding λI makes the matrix invertible for λ > 0
It standardizes the target variable
questions.why: X^T X is positive semi-definite, so adding λI shifts every eigenvalue up by λ, making the system positive definite and giving a unique, stable solution that splits weight across the collinear features. Dropping features is closer to Lasso's behavior, not ridge's.

questions.q: In XGBoost, the learning rate (eta) is reduced from 0.3 to 0.03. What adjustment is usually needed?
options: Reduce the number of trees by 10×
Increase the number of boosting rounds substantially, typically using early stopping on validation data
Increase the maximum tree depth to 50
No adjustment; eta only affects training speed
questions.why: Each tree's contribution is scaled by eta, so a smaller eta needs many more trees to reach the same fit but usually generalizes better. Very deep trees would increase overfitting rather than compensate for shrinkage.

questions.q: In a random forest trained with bootstrap sampling on a large dataset, roughly what fraction of training examples is left out of any given tree, enabling out-of-bag (OOB) evaluation?
questions.why: The chance that a given example is never drawn in n samples with replacement is (1 − 1/n)^n → e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368. The 63.2% figure is the fraction of unique examples that do appear in a bootstrap sample.

questions.q: Which step is required before computing principal components through the SVD of a data matrix X?
options: Center each feature by subtracting its mean
One-hot encode all numeric features
Sort the rows by their label
Apply softmax to each row
questions.why: Principal components are eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, which assumes centered data; without centering, the first component largely points toward the mean. Standardizing as well is advisable when features use very different units.

questions.q: A UMAP projection shows two clusters far apart and a third close to one of them. What can be safely concluded?
options: The two distant clusters are the most dissimilar in the original space, in proportion to the gap
The cluster sizes on the plot reflect their true variance
Local neighborhood structure is roughly preserved, but global inter-cluster distances and sizes are not reliable
UMAP output can be used directly as a linear projection like PCA
questions.why: t-SNE and UMAP are non-linear embeddings optimized mainly to keep nearby points nearby, so gaps and apparent sizes between clusters can be distorted. Both are available GPU-accelerated in cuML, which helps when running them repeatedly on large datasets.

questions.q: A classifier has ROC-AUC 0.95, but among cases where it predicts 0.9 probability only 60% are actually positive. How should this be fixed without retraining the model?
options: Lower the decision threshold to 0.5
Fit a calibration mapping such as temperature scaling, Platt scaling or isotonic regression on a held-out set
Increase the number of training epochs
Use accuracy instead of AUC
questions.why: The model ranks well (high AUC) but its probabilities are overconfident, which a post-hoc monotonic recalibration corrects without changing the ranking. Moving the threshold changes decisions, not whether a stated 0.9 really means 90%.

questions.q: A 5-class model is very accurate on two large classes but poor on three rare classes. Which F1 averaging best exposes the poor rare-class performance?
options: Micro-averaged F1
Accuracy
Weighted F1 by class support
Macro-averaged F1
questions.why: Macro-F1 computes F1 per class and takes an unweighted mean, so each rare class counts as much as each large one. Micro-F1 and support-weighted F1 are dominated by the large classes and would hide the problem.

questions.q: A model has precision 0.6 and recall 0.9. What is its F1 score?
questions.why: F1 = 2 × 0.6 × 0.9 / (0.6 + 0.9) = 1.08 / 1.5 = 0.72. The arithmetic mean, 0.75, overstates performance because it does not penalize the imbalance between precision and recall.

questions.q: A team replaces a high-cardinality "merchant_id" with the mean fraud rate per merchant, computed on the whole training set, and sees validation AUC collapse in production. What is the correct practice?
options: Compute the encoding on the test set instead
Use label encoding with random integers
Compute target encodings out-of-fold (or with smoothing) so a row's own label never contributes to its encoded value
Drop the validation set and train on all data
questions.why: When a row's label is part of its own feature, especially for rare merchants with few rows, the model learns to read the label back and overfits badly. Out-of-fold encoding plus smoothing toward the global mean prevents this self-leakage; encoding on the test set leaks even more directly.

questions.q: A team tunes hyperparameters with 5-fold CV and reports the best CV score as the expected production performance. Why is this optimistic, and what fixes it?
options: It is not optimistic; CV scores are always unbiased
Selecting the best configuration on the same folds biases the score upward; nested CV uses an outer loop for evaluation and an inner loop for tuning
5 folds are too many; use 2-fold CV
The score should be multiplied by (k − 1)/k
questions.why: Taking the maximum over many configurations evaluated on the same data picks up favorable noise. Nested CV (or a separate untouched test set) evaluates the entire tuning procedure on data it never saw.

questions.q: A loan-default model's input distribution changes because the bank enters a new region, but the relationship between applicant features and default stays the same. What is this?
options: Concept drift
Label noise
Target leakage
Covariate shift
questions.why: Covariate shift means P(x) changes while P(y | x) stays fixed, so importance weighting or retraining on new inputs can help. Concept drift is when P(y | x) itself changes, for example when an economic shock alters who defaults given the same features.

questions.q: Ignoring activations, roughly how much GPU memory does training a 1-billion-parameter model in pure FP32 with Adam require for weights, gradients and optimizer states?
options: 16 GB
4 GB
8 GB
12 GB
questions.why: Each parameter needs 4 bytes for the weight, 4 for its gradient and 8 for Adam's two moment estimates, which is 16 bytes × 1B = 16 GB. 4 GB is only the weights, which is enough for inference but not for training with Adam.

questions.q: Training with a very large batch size and the same number of epochs often converges to a solution with a noticeably worse validation score. Which explanation is commonly given?
options: Large batches always overflow FP16
Large batches use more dropout automatically
Less gradient noise and fewer updates tend to steer toward sharper minima that generalize worse, unless the learning rate and schedule are adjusted
Large batches make the training data smaller
questions.why: Small-batch gradient noise acts as an implicit regularizer, and large batches also perform fewer steps per epoch. Techniques such as learning-rate scaling with warmup or layer-wise adaptive optimizers (e.g., LAMB) narrow this gap; batch size does not change dropout or overflow behavior.

questions.q: Early in GAN training the discriminator becomes nearly perfect, and the generator stops improving. What is the underlying issue and a common remedy?
options: The generator overfits; add dropout to the generator
With the original minimax loss the generator's gradients vanish; use the non-saturating loss or a Wasserstein-style objective
The learning rate is too low for the discriminator; increase it further
The latent vector is too large; reduce it to one dimension
questions.why: When the discriminator confidently rejects fakes, log(1 − D(G(z))) saturates and gives almost no gradient. Maximizing log D(G(z)) instead, or using WGAN with a gradient penalty, gives informative gradients; strengthening the discriminator further would worsen the problem.

questions.q: Why do VAEs sample the latent as z = μ + σ·ε with ε ~ N(0, I) instead of sampling z ~ N(μ, σ²) directly?
options: It makes the latent space discrete
It removes the KL term from the loss
It eliminates randomness from training
It moves randomness into ε so gradients can flow through μ and σ to the encoder
questions.why: Sampling is not differentiable with respect to the distribution's parameters, but a deterministic transformation of external noise is. The sample is still random (option C is false) and the KL term remains part of the objective.

questions.q: In a standard DDPM, a clean image x₀ is noised as x_t = √ᾱ_t·x₀ + √(1 − ᾱ_t)·ε. What is the network typically trained to predict?
options: The noise ε that was added, using an MSE loss
The class label of x₀
The timestep t from x₀
Whether x_t is real or fake, using a discriminator loss
questions.why: The simplified DDPM loss is ‖ε − ε_θ(x_t, t)‖², which is mathematically linked to the variational bound and to score matching. Real-vs-fake discrimination is the GAN objective; diffusion models need no adversary.

questions.q: In a text-to-image diffusion model with classifier-free guidance, what is the usual effect of raising the guidance scale?
options: More diverse images with weaker prompt adherence
Fewer denoising steps are needed
Stronger prompt adherence at the cost of diversity, with artifacts at very high scales
No change unless a separate classifier is trained
questions.why: CFG extrapolates from the unconditional prediction toward the conditional one: ε̂ = ε_uncond + w·(ε_cond − ε_uncond), where the same network is trained with the condition randomly dropped. It needs no separate classifier, unlike earlier classifier guidance, and it does not reduce the step count.

questions.q: What distinguishes normalizing flows from GANs and VAEs?
options: They generate data by iterative denoising
They use invertible transformations, so the exact data likelihood can be computed via the change-of-variables formula
They require an adversarial discriminator
They can only model discrete data
questions.why: Flows map a simple base distribution through invertible layers whose Jacobian determinants are tractable, giving exact log-likelihoods. GANs give no likelihood at all, and VAEs optimize only a lower bound (the ELBO).

questions.q: Autoregressive sequence models are usually trained by feeding the ground-truth previous tokens as input. What issue can this cause at generation time?
options: The model cannot be parallelized during training
The model never learns to predict the first token
Training loss cannot be computed with cross-entropy
Exposure bias: at inference the model conditions on its own possibly erroneous outputs, a distribution it never saw in training
questions.why: Teacher forcing makes training stable and lets all positions be computed in parallel (so option A is backwards), but small early mistakes at inference can compound. Scheduled sampling and sequence-level training objectives are attempts to reduce this mismatch.

questions.q: A schedule warms up linearly from 0 to a peak learning rate of 3 × 10⁻⁴ over the first 1,000 steps. What is the learning rate at step 250?
questions.why: Linear warmup gives lr = peak × step / warmup_steps = 3 × 10⁻⁴ × 250 / 1,000 = 7.5 × 10⁻⁵. The peak value (option B) is reached only at step 1,000.

questions.q: A pipeline prepares features in cuDF and then trains a PyTorch model on the same GPU. How can the data move between libraries without copying through host memory?
options: Export the DataFrame to CSV and reload it in PyTorch
Convert to a pandas DataFrame and then to a NumPy array
Use DLPack or the CUDA Array Interface to share the GPU buffers directly
Serialize the DataFrame with pickle
questions.why: RAPIDS, CuPy and PyTorch support these standard protocols for exchanging device memory, so tensors can be handed off without a GPU → CPU → GPU round trip. Going through pandas/NumPy forces a host copy, adding latency for large datasets.

questions.q: What does the universal approximation theorem guarantee about a feedforward network with one hidden layer and a suitable non-linear activation?
options: Gradient descent will always find the best approximation
With enough hidden units, it can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain to arbitrary accuracy
A small hidden layer is sufficient for any task
Deep networks are unnecessary in practice
questions.why: The theorem is purely about representational capacity: it says nothing about how many units are needed, whether training will find the right weights, or how well the result generalizes. In practice deeper networks often represent functions far more efficiently than a single wide layer.

questions.q: For squared-error loss, how does the expected test error at a point decompose?
options: Bias + variance
Bias² × variance + noise
Training error + validation error
Bias² + variance + irreducible noise
questions.why: The expected squared error splits into squared bias (systematic error), variance (sensitivity to the training sample) and noise that no model can remove. Option A forgets both the square on bias and the irreducible noise floor that bounds achievable error.
